transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-09
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Jared Mills (Echo Labs CTO), Nina Alvarez (PM), Marcus Lee (ML Eng)

[00:00] Samir (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we have about 50 minutes, wanted to run through Echo Labs' usage patterns, your budget constraints, and then talk through hosted vs dedicated vs private onramps — and importantly cost per token levers like batching and caching. priya will jump into the bench plan after i get context.

[00:15] Jared (Echo): cool thanks samir. quick context: we've got a chat assistant being baked into our developer portal, expect steady ramp. baseline today is about 1.2M tokens per day in devcamp tests, spike patterns around releases. latencies need to be p95 < 400ms for single-turn queries. budget is, um, roughly $18k/month initially for inference.

[00:40] Nina (Echo): and security wise, we're PCI-adjacent and have to be careful about residency for some customers. SSO with SAML and audit logs are must-haves.

[01:05] Samir: perfect — that budget/latency combo is exactly the tradeoff we see. two immediate axes: per-token unit price (hosted), and infrastructure amortization (dedicated/reserved). priya, quick overview of levers?

[01:20] Priya (Redwood): yeah so high level — you can tune unit economics via three primary levers: batching (more tokens per request), KV/prefix caching (reduces generation tokens), and model variant/quantization choices. e.g., moving from float16 to an int8 quantized variant often reduces GPU cost 20–40% depending on model. caching is big for sessiony workloads — if you have repeated prefixes we can shave off 30–60% of generation tokens.

[01:55] Marcus (Echo): we do a lot of repeated prompts — template-heavy. so caching could be high impact. what about batching impact on latency? we can't add 200ms.

[02:10] Priya: right — batching increases throughput but adds wait time to batch fill. Redwood's runtime supports latency SLO-based batching: it will only batch up to a latency cap you set. so if your p95 400ms is strict, we can set max queue delay to 30–50ms and still get useful batching for small models. for big models with long token gen, the benefit is different. also continuous batching for streaming tokens reduces per-token kernel overhead.

[02:48] Jared: ok that makes sense. can we get example unit econ — like per-1k-token hosted price vs dedicated breakdown?

[03:00] Samir: absolutely — i'll send a pilot pricing sheet. quick numbers off the cuff: hosted per-1k-token for our verified open model family ranges by model — for a mid-sized 7B-ish variant it's roughly $0.02–$0.035 per 1k tokens at baseline. dedicated can push that to $0.006–$0.015 per 1k tokens after you amortize reserved capacity and apply batching/caching. those are ballpark — final depends on concurrency, token length distribution.

[03:30] Nina: that's a big delta. how long to reach dedicated? we don't have multi-million daily tokens yet.

[03:45] Priya: typically we recommend a 3–6 month pilot on hosted with a dedicated eval period once you hit commit thresholds (we can show model throughput and expected burn). Redwood Dedicated has reserved pools; you can start with burst-enabled reserved capacity to keep costs predictable. there's also a hybrid routing option — default requests on hosted, high-volume routes on dedicated.

[04:12] Marcus: can you mimic our workload for the pilot? our tokens skew short — average 45 tokens per request, but some synthesis flows go to 600 tokens.

[04:30] Priya: yes, please send anonymized traces. we'll run two benchmark scenarios: steady-state (45 tokens) and spike/synthesis (600 tokens). for steady-state we focus on batching window and queue-delay effects. for long tokens we watch kernel execution and memory (kv cache pressure).

[05:00] Jared: speaking of KV cache, earlier you mentioned cache savings — how predictable is that? sometimes our templates change and the cache hit rate drops.

[05:15] Priya: cache hit depends on prefix repeatability. for developer portals with templates, it's usually high. we provide tools to measure prefix similarity and expected cache hit. also Redwood's caching works across requests within a session and can persist some prefixes depending on privacy configs. for sensitive data we can turn off cross-user persistence.

[05:48] Nina: what about compliance — KMS, HSM, SOC2 — we need to know you'll integrate with our key mgmt if we go private.

[06:00] Samir: we have SOC2 and can integrate with customer KMS; Private deployment includes customer-controlled KMS/HSM and on-prem options. we'll share the security package — i'll include it in the follow-up.

[06:20] Marcus: latency targets — if we set p95 400ms, what's typical for hosted on 7B vs dedicated?

[06:35] Priya: typical hosted p95 for 7B generation of 100 tokens is 150–300ms depending on concurrency. Dedicated with optimized batching and kernel selection can lower steady-state p95 by 10–30% and reduce jitter. but dedicated requires tuning: larger batch sizes for peak throughput but that may push median latency down while p95 could be influenced by spikes.

[07:10] Jared: curious about fallbacks — if dedicated pool is saturated during a launch day, can requests fallback to hosted?

[07:20] Samir: yes, smart routing supports fallback to hosted or to a cheaper model variant. you can configure policy: failover to hosted with throttling or to a quantized variant. that ensures uptime but may change output quality. we track rerouting metrics in the console.

[07:40] Nina: on pricing — how do you treat cache-saved tokens? are they billed?

[07:48] Samir: good question — caching reduces generation tokens; billing is based on tokens actually generated plus a small inference request overhead. so if caching removes 50% of generated tokens, your billed generation tokens go down accordingly. we'll show example spreadsheets.

[08:05] Marcus: for the benchmark, can you show both per-request cost and aggregated monthly projection for our traffic shape?

[08:12] Priya: yes. please include trace, target SLOs, and an expected ramp profile. we'll run bench, export per-token timing and cost numbers and then feed that into a simple unit-econ model to show monthly burn under hosted vs dedicated vs private.

[08:35] Jared: what about concurrency limits and cold-starts? we're serverless on our side and would like autoscaling to be smooth.

[08:45] Priya: Redwood's runtime is designed for high-throughput and warm KV caches; cold-starts mainly happen on model load. Dedicated keeps a pool of warm GPUs for pinned models. hosted can have cold-starts if model hasn't been used recently; we can pin to reduce that in Hosted but that's essentially dedicated-like. we'll account for model load time in the bench.

[09:10] Samir: quick note — competitors like Anthropic/OpenAI have simpler hosted pricing but fewer knobs for batching/caching at the infra level. Redwood's differentiation is the telemetry and the levers you can apply.

[09:30] Nina: ok good. let's talk pilot scope and acceptance criteria. we'd want: 1) demonstration of sustained throughput x/sec for our steady-state, 2) p95 < 400ms, 3) unit cost improvement estimate to justify moving to dedicated at a predicted volume.

[09:55] Samir: that sounds right. proposal: two-week hosted pilot to collect traces + run bench, then a 2–4 week dedicated eval with reserved pool if numbers justify it. pilot deliverables: bench report, unit-econ spreadsheet, recommended routing policy.

[10:20] Marcus: curious — for private deployment there's a vendor integration effort, any idea of lead times?

[10:30] Priya: Private (VPC/on-prem) typically is 6–10 weeks depending on access and network policies. we do a security review, then deployment and validation. for time to value, most customers do hosted->dedicated->private.

[10:55] Jared: ok. price sensitivity — if we need to cap spend to $18k/mo max, what are options?

[11:05] Samir: you can cap spend by routing 80% low-cost workload to cached/quantized variants and keep high-quality outputs for 20% of traffic. also rate limiting, token quotas per API key, and cost alerts. we can simulate the cap in the unit-econ model.

[11:30] Nina: any gotchas in token accounting we should know? we've seen differences between request vs generated tokens across vendors.

[11:38] Priya: yes, count differences exist — we report request tokens, generated tokens, and billed tokens separately. we'll show mapping and sample logs. transcript note: occasionally transcript auto-puts weird tokens like K V cash instead of KV cache.

[12:00] Jared: great. i think we're aligned. next steps?

[12:08] Samir: recap and actions: 1) Samir will send pilot pricing sheet + security package + sample unit-econ spreadsheet by 2026-03-11. 2) Echo to upload traces by 2026-03-10. 3) Priya to run 2-hr benchmark and share numbers by 2026-03-12. 4) schedule follow-up technical deep dive week of Mar 16.

[12:35] Nina: noted. also we'll flag legal for reviewing data residency for pilot.

[12:45] Marcus: posting a note — i'll anonymize the traces and put them in the drive after this call.

[12:53] Samir: awesome. thanks all, we'll follow up by email. end.

Meeting end.
